claim: Bacteria often live in biofilms, which are microbial communities surrounded by a secreted extracellular matrix.
source: Bacteria often live in biofilms, which are microbial communities surrounded by a secreted extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in microbiology supported by scientific consensus.

claim: In competition with matrix mutants, wild-type P. aeruginosa cells always increase in relative abundance in planar microfluidic devices under simple flow regimes, irrespective of initial frequency.
source: Irrespective of initial frequency, in competition with matrix mutants, wild-type cells always increase in relative abundance in planar microfluidic devices under simple flow regimes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1A,B showing wild-type PA14 increased in relative abundance regardless of initial population composition in planar chambers.

claim: In microenvironments with complex, irregular flow profiles, wild-type matrix-producing and isogenic non-producing P. aeruginosa strains can coexist.
source: By contrast, in microenvironments with complex, irregular flow profiles – which are common in natural environments – wild-type matrix-producing and isogenic non-producing strains can coexist.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C demonstrating negative frequency-dependent selection in column-containing chambers.

claim: Local obstruction of flow by wild-type matrix producers generates regions of near-zero shear that allow matrix mutants to locally accumulate.
source: This result stems from local obstruction of flow by wild-type matrix producers, which generates regions of near-zero shear that allow matrix mutants to locally accumulate.
evidence: This is supported by flow tracking experiments and spatial distribution analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: In nature, bacteria predominantly exist in biofilms, which are surface-attached or free-floating communities of cells held together by a secreted matrix.
source: In nature, bacteria predominantly exist in biofilms, which are surface-attached or free-floating communities of cells held together by a secreted matrix (Hall-Stoodley et al., 2004; Nadell et al., 2009; Flemming et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The extracellular matrix defines biofilm structure, promotes cell-cell and cell-surface adhesion, and confers resistance to chemical and physical insults.
source: The extracellular matrix defines biofilm structure, promotes cell-cell and cell-surface adhesion, and confers resistance to chemical and physical insults (Flemming and Wingender, 2010; Hobley et al., 2015; Teschler et al., 2015; Tseng et al., 2013; Doroshenko et al., 2014; Landry et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The matrix plays a role in the social evolution and population dynamics of biofilm-dwelling bacteria.
source: The matrix also plays a role in the social evolution and population dynamics of biofilm-dwelling bacteria (Nadell et al., 2009; Steenackers et al., 2016; Nadell et al., 2016; Ghoul and Mitri, 2016; Mitri et al., 2016, 2013, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: In Bacillus subtilis, matrix materials are readily shared among cells, leading to public goods dilemmas in which non-producing strains can outcompete producing strains.
source: In some species, such as the soil bacterium Bacillus subtilis, matrix materials are readily shared among cells, leading to public goods dilemmas in which non-producing strains can outcompete producing strains (van Gestel et al., 2015, 2014; Kovács, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature on B. subtilis.

claim: In Vibrio cholerae, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and P. aeruginosa, matrix-secreting cell lineages privatize most matrix components, allowing them to smother or laterally displace other cell lineages and outcompete non-producing cells.
source: In other species, including the pathogens Vibrio cholerae, Pseudomonas fluorescens, and P. aeruginosa, matrix-secreting cell lineages privatize most matrix components, allowing them to smother or laterally displace other cell lineages and, in so doing, outcompete non-producing cells (Xavier and Foster, 2007; Nadell and Bassler, 2011; Nadell et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2014c; Schluter et al., 2015; Irie et al., 2016; Drescher et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016; Madsen et al., 2015; Oliveira et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Not all wild and clinical isolates of V. cholerae, P. fluorescens, and P. aeruginosa produce a biofilm matrix, despite the clear ecological and competitive benefits of possessing a matrix.
source: Interestingly, not all wild and clinical isolates of these species produce a biofilm matrix, despite the clear ecological and competitive benefits of possessing a matrix (Mann and Wozniak, 2012; Yawata et al., 2014; Chowdhury et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Constrained movement can promote coexistence of different bacterial strains and species in colonies on agar.
source: Theory and experiments investigating bacterial colonies on agar show that constrained movement can promote coexistence of different strains and species (Levin, 1974; Levin and Paine, 1974; Durrett and Levin, 1994, 1998; Kerr et al., 2002; Kim et al., 2008; Poltak and Cooper, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior theoretical and experimental work.

claim: Fitness trade-offs between the benefits of being adhered to surfaces and the ability to disperse to new locations can cause variability in matrix production.
source: Fitness trade-offs between the benefits of being adhered to surfaces and the ability to disperse to new locations can cause variability in matrix production (Nadell and Bassler, 2011; Yawata et al., 2014; Levin, 1974; Cohen and Levin, 1991), but it is not well understood how selective forces within the biofilm environment itself might drive the coexistence of strains that make matrix with strains that do not.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Local hydrodynamics associated with natural environments can have dramatic effects on biofilm matrix organization.
source: The local hydrodynamics associated with natural environments can have dramatic effects on biofilm matrix organization.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and the subsequent discussion of P. aeruginosa biofilm structures under different flow conditions.

claim: P. aeruginosa is a common soil bacterium.
source: This phenomenon has been particularly well established for P. aeruginosa, a common soil bacterium (Green et al., 1974) and opportunistic pathogen that thrives in open wounds (Fazli et al., 2009; Burmølle et al., 2010), on sub-epithelial medical devices (Guaglianone et al., 2010), and in the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients (Harmsen et al., 2010; Ciofu et al., 2013; Folkesson et al., 2012; Stacy et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: P. aeruginosa is an opportunistic pathogen that thrives in open wounds, on sub-epithelial medical devices, and in the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients.
source: This phenomenon has been particularly well established for P. aeruginosa, a common soil bacterium (Green et al., 1974) and opportunistic pathogen that thrives in open wounds (Fazli et al., 2009; Burmølle et al., 2010), on sub-epithelial medical devices (Guaglianone et al., 2010), and in the lungs of cystic fibrosis patients (Harmsen et al., 2010; Ciofu et al., 2013; Folkesson et al., 2012; Stacy et al., 2015; McNally et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Under steady laminar flow in simple microfluidic channels, P. aeruginosa forms biofilms with intermittent mushroom-shaped tower structures.
source: Under steady laminar flow in simple microfluidic channels, P. aeruginosa forms biofilms with intermittent mushroom-shaped tower structures (Harmsen et al., 2010; Friedman and Kolter, 2004; Miller et al., 2012; Parsek and Tolker-Nielsen, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Under irregular flow regimes in complex environments, P. aeruginosa produces sieve-like biofilm streamers that protrude into the liquid phase above the substratum.
source: Under irregular flow regimes in more complex environments, however, P. aeruginosa also produces sieve-like biofilm streamers that protrude into the liquid phase above the substratum (Persat et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2014a, 2014b; Rusconi et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: P. aeruginosa streamers are proficient at catching cells, nutrients, and debris that pass by, leading to clogging and termination of local flow.
source: These streamers – whose structure depends on the secreted matrix – are proficient at catching cells, nutrients, and debris that pass by, leading to clogging and termination of local flow (Drescher et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Pel is a viscoelastic matrix polysaccharide that serves as the primary structural element for P. aeruginosa PA14 biofilm and streamer formation.
source: Here, we study within-biofilm competition as a function of flow regime using strains of P. aeruginosa PA14 that differ only in their production of Pel, a viscoelastic matrix polysaccharide that serves as the primary structural element for biofilm and streamer formation (Friedman and Kolter, 2004; Drescher et al., 2013; Chew et al., 2014; Jennings et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of pelA is required for synthesis of Pel in P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: We performed competition experiments with wild type PA14 and an otherwise isogenic strain deleted for pelA, which is required for synthesis of Pel (Franklin et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Deletion of pelA significantly impairs biofilm formation in PA14.
source: Deletion of pelA significantly impairs biofilm formation in PA14, which does not naturally produce Psl, an additional matrix polysaccharide secreted by other P. aeruginosa isolates (Colvin et al., 2012, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PA14 does not naturally produce Psl, an additional matrix polysaccharide secreted by other P. aeruginosa isolates.
source: Deletion of pelA significantly impairs biofilm formation in PA14, which does not naturally produce Psl, an additional matrix polysaccharide secreted by other P. aeruginosa isolates (Colvin et al., 2012, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fluorescent protein expression constructs (GFP or mCherry) had no measurable effect on growth rate of P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: Experiments in shaken liquid culture using genetically identical wild-type cells producing GFP or mCherry confirmed that fluorescent protein expression constructs had no measurable effect on growth rate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Pel is necessary for streamer formation under complex flow regimes in P. aeruginosa PA14.
source: We focused on Pel because it is the key structural polysaccharide in PA14 biofilms, and it is necessary for streamer formation under complex flow regimes.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge from prior studies and the experimental design of the current study.

claim: In planar chambers with simple parabolic flows, wild-type PA14 increased in relative abundance regardless of initial population composition.
source: In planar chambers with simple parabolic flows, wild-type PA14 increased in relative abundance regardless of initial population composition, indicating uniform positive selection for Pel secretion (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The result that wild-type PA14 outcompetes ΔpelA in planar chambers is consistent with recent studies of V. cholerae and Pseudomonas spp. demonstrating that core structural polysaccharides of the secreted matrix cannot be readily exploited by non-producing mutants.
source: This result is consistent with recent studies of V. cholerae and Pseudomonas spp. demonstrating that – in these species – core structural polysaccharides of the secreted matrix cannot be readily exploited by non-producing mutants (Nadell and Bassler, 2011; Nadell et al., 2015; Kim et al., 2014c; Schluter et al., 2015; Irie et al., 2016; Yan et al., 2016; Madsen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and inference from the current experimental results.

claim: Pel-producers mostly excluded non-Pel-producing cells from biofilm clusters in planar chambers.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed that Pel-producers mostly excluded non-Pel-producing cells from biofilm clusters in planar chambers (Figure 2A,B), although some ∆pelA mutants resided on the periphery of wild-type biofilms.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Some ΔpelA mutants resided on the periphery of wild-type biofilms in planar chambers.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed that Pel-producers mostly excluded non-Pel-producing cells from biofilm clusters in planar chambers (Figure 2A,B), although some ∆pelA mutants resided on the periphery of wild-type biofilms.
evidence: This claim is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The liquid effluent from planar chambers contained an over-representation of the ΔpelA mutant relative to wild type.
source: The liquid effluent from these chambers contained an over-representation of the ∆pelA mutant relative to wild type, consistent with the interpretation that ∆pelA strain was displaced from the substratum over time (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The ΔpelA strain was displaced from the substratum over time in planar chambers.
source: The liquid effluent from these chambers contained an over-representation of the ∆pelA mutant relative to wild type, consistent with the interpretation that ∆pelA strain was displaced from the substratum over time (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the effluent data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In microfluidic devices simulating porous microenvironments, there was a pronounced shift to negative frequency-dependent selection for Pel production.
source: When wild-type and ∆pelA cells competed in microfluidic devices simulating porous microenvironments, by contrast, there was a pronounced shift to negative frequency-dependent selection for Pel production (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: Wild-type PA14 was selectively favored at initial frequencies below ~0.6 in porous microenvironments.
source: Wild-type PA14 was selectively favored at initial frequencies below ~0.6.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: Above a critical frequency of ~0.6, the ΔpelA mutant was favored in porous microenvironments.
source: Above this critical frequency, the ∆pelA mutant was favored.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: In porous environments, ΔpelA null mutants can grow and stably coexist with wild type Pel-producers.
source: From this result, we can infer that in this porous environment, ∆pelA null mutants can grow and stably coexist with wild type Pel-producers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the negative frequency-dependent selection data shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: Streamers were produced by wild-type P. aeruginosa cells in column-containing chambers but not planar chambers.
source: In our experiments, streamers were produced by wild-type cells and could be readily detected via microscopy throughout column-containing chambers, but not planar chambers.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations in the experiments.

claim: ΔpelA cells were not abundant in streamers produced by wild-type cells.
source: Streamers are known to catch cells and debris that pass by (Drescher et al., 2013), and although ∆pelA cells could be found in the streamers in our experiments, they were not abundant.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cell capture by streamers cannot account for the observed coexistence of wild-type and ΔpelA strains.
source: Cell capture by streamers therefore cannot account for the observed coexistence of the two strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ΔpelA cells were not abundant in streamers.

claim: Streamers catch debris.
source: This result suggests that streamers do indeed catch debris, consistent with prior studies (Kim et al., 2014b; Drescher et al., 2013), but that in our system, ∆pelA cells are not present at high enough density in the passing liquid phase to accumulate substantial population sizes by this mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and observations in the current study.

claim: In the experimental system, ΔpelA cells are not present at high enough density in the passing liquid phase to accumulate substantial population sizes by streamer capture.
source: This result suggests that streamers do indeed catch debris, consistent with prior studies (Kim et al., 2014b; Drescher et al., 2013), but that in our system, ∆pelA cells are not present at high enough density in the passing liquid phase to accumulate substantial population sizes by this mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that ΔpelA cells were not abundant in streamers despite streamers catching debris.

claim: Wild-type biofilms gradually obstructed some of the regions located between columns over time in chambers containing column obstacles.
source: Our microscopy-based observation of chambers containing column obstacles suggested that wild-type biofilms gradually obstructed some of the regions located between columns over time.
evidence: This claim is supported by microscopy observations in the experiments.

claim: The ΔpelA strain is sensitive to removal by shear.
source: We hypothesized that partial clogging could render those portions of the chambers more suitable for growth of the ∆pelA strain, which was previously shown to be sensitive to removal by shear (Colvin et al., 2012, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: ΔpelA cells should be found predominantly in regions of the chamber that have been clogged by wild type biofilms.
source: This hypothesis predicts that ∆pelA cells should be found predominantly in regions of the chamber that have been clogged by wild type biofilms.
evidence: This is a prediction based on the hypothesis that clogging reduces shear and the ΔpelA strain is sensitive to shear.

claim: ΔpelA biofilm clusters occurred significantly more often in regions in which flow was blocked by wild-type biofilms than in regions in which flow was not interrupted.
source: Importantly, and in support of our prediction, ∆pelA biofilm clusters occurred significantly more often in regions in which flow was blocked by wild-type biofilms than in regions in which flow was not interrupted (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: ΔpelA cells did not clog chambers when grown in isolation.
source: As shown previously (Drescher et al., 2013), ∆pelA cells did not clog chambers when grown in isolation, supporting the interpretation that ∆pelA accumulation relies on and only occurs after clogging by the wild type.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and observations in the current study.

claim: ΔpelA accumulation relies on and only occurs after clogging by the wild type.
source: As shown previously (Drescher et al., 2013), ∆pelA cells did not clog chambers when grown in isolation, supporting the interpretation that ∆pelA accumulation relies on and only occurs after clogging by the wild type.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the observation that ΔpelA cells did not clog chambers when grown alone.

claim: Pel-producers have higher shear tolerance than Pel-deficient cells.
source: This result is consistent with prior indications that Pel-producers have higher shear tolerance than Pel-deficient cells (Colvin et al., 2012, 2011), which we confirmed in our system by growing each strain in isolation under varying shear stress in planar chambers (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The ΔpelA strain can outcompete the wild type when the two are grown together in planar microfluidic chambers in the absence of flow.
source: Further supporting our interpretation, the ∆pelA strain can outcompete the wild type when the two are grown together in planar microfluidic chambers in the absence of flow (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The absence of flow approximates the clogged areas of complex flow environments.
source: This experiment approximates the clogged areas of complex flow environments, and the results explain how – on spatial scales encompassing areas of high flow and low or no flow – the wild-type and the ∆pelA strains can coexist.
evidence: This is an inference connecting the no-flow experiment to the complex flow environment observations.

claim: On spatial scales encompassing areas of high flow and low or no flow, the wild-type and the ΔpelA strains can coexist.
source: This experiment approximates the clogged areas of complex flow environments, and the results explain how – on spatial scales encompassing areas of high flow and low or no flow – the wild-type and the ∆pelA strains can coexist.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined results from flow and no-flow experiments.

claim: Biofilm growth is ubiquitous in porous microenvironments and often causes clogging in natural and industrial contexts, including soil beds and water filtration systems.
source: Biofilm growth is ubiquitous in porous microenvironments and often causes clogging in natural and industrial contexts, including soil beds and water filtration systems (Knowles et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The clogging process can dramatically influence population dynamics within growing biofilms by generating a feedback between hydrodynamic flow, biofilm spatial architecture, and competition.
source: Here, we have shown that the clogging process can dramatically influence population dynamics within growing biofilms by generating a feedback between hydrodynamic flow, biofilm spatial architecture, and competition (Coyte et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental results presented in the manuscript and a citation to related work.

claim: When P. aeruginosa wild type and ΔpelA mutants experience irregular flow in heterogeneous environments, wild-type biofilm formation causes partial clogging, regionally reducing local flow speed.
source: Our findings suggest that when P. aeruginosa wild type and ΔpelA mutants experience irregular flow in heterogeneous environments, wild-type biofilm formation causes partial clogging, regionally reducing local flow speed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing flow obstruction and spatial distribution of strains.

claim: The lack of flow generates favorable conditions for the ΔpelA strain, whose biofilms would otherwise be removed by shear forces.
source: The lack of flow generates favorable conditions for the ∆pelA strain, whose biofilms would otherwise be removed by shear forces, presumably enabling it to proliferate locally if sufficient nutrients for growth diffuse from other areas of the chamber in which medium continues to flow (Bottero et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results and a citation to related work on nutrient diffusion.

claim: P. aeruginosa is notorious as an opportunistic pathogen of plants and animals, including humans.
source: P. aeruginosa is notorious as an opportunistic pathogen of plants and animals, including humans (Xavier, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: P. aeruginosa thrives outside of hosts in porous niches such as soil.
source: It also thrives outside of hosts, for example, in porous niches such as soil (Fierer et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Environmental and clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa exhibit considerable variation in their production of matrix components, including loss or overexpression of Pel.
source: Despite the well-documented ecological benefits of matrix secretion during biofilm formation, environmental and clinical isolates of P. aeruginosa exhibit considerable variation in their production of matrix components, including loss or overexpression of Pel (Mann and Wozniak, 2012; Chew et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The evolutionary stable states of extracellular matrix secretion vary with the topographical complexity of the flow environment in which the bacteria reside.
source: Our results offer an explanation for natural variation in the ability of P. aeruginosa to produce extracellular matrix, particularly among bacteria in porous microhabitats: the evolutionary stable states of extracellular matrix secretion vary with the topographical complexity of the flow environment in which the bacteria reside.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental results showing different competitive outcomes in simple versus complex flow environments.

claim: All strains used in the study are derivatives of Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14.
source: All strains are derivatives of Pseudomonas aeruginosa PA14 (RRID:WB_PA14).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the strains used in the study.

claim: Wild-type PA14 strains constitutively producing fluorescent proteins harbor genes encoding either EGFP or mCherry under the control of the PA1/04/03 promoter in single copy on the chromosome.
source: Wild-type PA14 strains constitutively producing fluorescent proteins (Drescher et al., 2013) were provided by Albert Siryaporn (UC Irvine), and they harbor genes encoding either EGFP or mCherry under the control of the PA1/04/03 promoter in single copy on the chromosome (Choi and Schweizer, 2006).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the genetic constructs used in the study, supported by citations.

claim: The ΔpelA strain was constructed using the lambda red system modified for P. aeruginosa.
source: The ∆pelA strain was constructed using the lambda red system modified for P. aeruginosa (Lesic and Rahme, 2008).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the method used to construct the mutant strain, supported by a citation.

claim: The maximum growth rates of wild-type cells expressing GFP and wild-type cells expressing mCherry were not different.
source: The maximum growth rates of wild-type cells expressing GFP and wild-type cells expressing mCherry were not different, indicating that the fluorescent protein constructs did not introduce growth rate bias (two-sample t = 0.235, df = 6, p=0.822).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental growth rate data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Microfluidic devices consisting of PDMS bonded to glass slides were constructed using standard soft photolithography techniques.
source: Microfluidic devices consisting of poly(dimethylsiloxane) (PDMS) bonded to 36 mm x 60 mm glass slides were constructed using standard soft photolithography techniques (Sia and Whitesides, 2003).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methods used, supported by a citation.

claim: The average flow speed in the experiments was 150–200 µm/s.
source: In our experiments, the average flow speed was 150–200 µm/s, unless noted otherwise.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental conditions.

claim: The size and spatial distributions of column obstacles were determined by taking a cross-section through a simulated volume of packed beads mimicking a simple soil environment.
source: The size and spatial distributions of these column obstacles were determined by taking a cross-section through a simulated volume of packed beads mimicking a simple soil environment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the design of the microfluidic chambers.

claim: Column radii in the soil-mimicking microfluidic devices varied from 80 to 200 μm, corresponding to particle sizes of fine- and medium-grain sand.
source: To convert the arbitrarily sized spheres from the 3D model to the actual sizes of physical columns in our microfluidic chambers, we chose column radii that varied from 80 to 200 μm, corresponding to particle sizes of fine- and medium-grain sand.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the design specifications of the microfluidic chambers.

claim: Imaging of biofilms could only be performed once for each experiment due to phototoxicity effects after multiple rounds of imaging.
source: Imaging of biofilms could only be performed once for each experiment, precluding time-series analyses, due to phototoxicity effects after multiple rounds of imaging.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental limitations.

claim: Phototoxicity was a particularly notable issue due to dimness of the fluorescent proteins in P. aeruginosa, which made long exposures necessary.
source: Phototoxicity was a particularly notable issue here due to dimness of the fluorescent proteins in P. aeruginosa, which made long exposures necessary to capture images of sufficient quality for later analysis.
evidence: This is a direct statement explaining the experimental challenge.

claim: Microfluidic experiments in the obstacle-containing chambers experience a high failure rate, in which no biofilms appear to grow after the 72 hr period of the experiment.
source: It should be noted that microfluidic experiments in the obstacle-containing chambers experience a high failure rate, in which no biofilms appear to grow after the 72 hr period of the experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental challenges.

claim: There is no significant difference in wild type occurrence in regions in which flow is unobstructed and in regions in which flow is blocked.
source: There is no significant difference in wild type occurrence in regions in which flow is unobstructed and in regions in which flow is blocked (two-sample t = 0.995, df = 4, p=0.376), but the ∆pelA strain is significantly more likely to occur in regions in which flow is blocked at a p<0.05 threshold with Bonferroni correction for two pairwise comparisons (two-sample t = 3.60, df = 4, p=0.0227).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The ΔpelA strain is significantly more likely to occur in regions in which flow is blocked at a p<0.05 threshold with Bonferroni correction for two pairwise comparisons.
source: There is no significant difference in wild type occurrence in regions in which flow is unobstructed and in regions in which flow is blocked (two-sample t = 0.995, df = 4, p=0.376), but the ∆pelA strain is significantly more likely to occur in regions in which flow is blocked at a p<0.05 threshold with Bonferroni correction for two pairwise comparisons (two-sample t = 3.60, df = 4, p=0.0227).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3B.
